text: No reliable rules exist by which an inexperienced person can judge the quality of leather with certainty; only long experience that trains the eye and touch is a safe guide.
A hide taken from an old and poor animal gives leather with a coarse, uneven, irregular grain, a hard and rough neck, thick and flabby flanks, and thin, baggy shoulders and hips.
A hide taken from a young, well-kept animal usually gives leather with a fine, close, even grain, a smooth flesh side of good color, and nearly uniform thickness over the whole side.
Grub holes are a sure indication of a poor hide, and they are easily detected.

To test for short tannage, cut a strip from the hide and wet the freshly cut edge with the tongue. If the color is uniform throughout and the cut edge looks smooth and glassy instead of being covered with fine fibres, the tannage is good.

Insufficiently tanned leather shows a fuzzy cut edge that feels harsh and rough when dry, and when wet it shows a white or light-colored strip through the center. The wider this light strip, the poorer the tannage.
Faults caused by bad currying are much harder to detect than faults caused by short tannage.
Strong acid blacks give leather a deep black color but make the grain hard and brittle.

To test whether the grain is hard and brittle, bend a narrow strip with the flesh sides together and close it down between the teeth. A hard, brittle grain breaks off short and shows the natural color of the leather underneath.
On extra heavy leather the bending test is likely to rupture the grain whether the quality is good or bad, but good leather looks torn asunder instead of broken off short.
If a hard grain was produced by strong acids that burned it, a freshly cut edge shows how deep they penetrated, with black streaks running well down into the fibres below the grain.
Impure oils or grease used in currying cause gum spots to appear on the surface, usually only after the harness has been made up and exposed for a time in the showcase.
If gum spots appear on the grain before the side has been cut, the leather can be treated by the recurrying method (soaking, tallowing and slicking), which prevents future gumming.
Good harness leather, in the words of an experienced leather dealer, should be "solid, but not hard; mellow, but not soft".
Three kinds of leather are used by harness makers in the United States: oak tanned, hemlock tanned, and union tanned.
Union leather is leather tanned with both oak and hemlock: either tanned with mixed oak and hemlock liquors, or first tanned with hemlock and afterwards retanned with oak.
All other conditions being equal, oak-tanned leather is by far the best leather for harness.

Oak-tanned leather is firmer but not as hard as hemlock, has a finer and denser fibre, is less affected by water, works up finer, takes a better finish, and has more strength and pliability than any other tannage.
Hemlock leather is harder than oak leather and has a dark red color, which interferes with its taking a good black and makes the black turn a dingy brown on exposure to the elements.

Hemlock leather has a more open and coarser-looking grain, wets up quickly, does not dry out as soft as oak leather, is harder to stitch, and is inferior in strength, particularly where the strain comes on a short bend or on the edge.
A side of hemlock leather weighs from eight to ten per cent more than a side of oak leather of equal spread and thickness.
Because hemlock leather is eight to ten per cent heavier than oak leather of the same size, the extra weight makes up for the margin in price between the two kinds.
Retanning hemlock-tanned leather with oak gives it a much lighter color, sometimes light enough on the flesh side to deceive a buyer who does not know union leather.
Union leather has a close grain that is as a rule finer than either oak or hemlock, but for harness it is inferior to oak in every respect and only a little better than hemlock.
Union leather weighs nearly as heavy as hemlock leather.
Hemlock leather should be preferred over oak leather in only one case: when the choice lies between inferior oak and superior hemlock.

The hides best suited for harness leather are those of young steers or heifers that were in the best condition when killed, because only they have fineness of grain, uniformity of thickness, and strength of fibre.
A cow hide is unfit for harness leather because the butt is liable to be thick and the shoulder thin.
A bullock hide is unfit for harness leather because it is thick at the head and belly and thin and soft at the butt.
Scratches on a hide are very injurious because they cannot be entirely removed and will show on the grain as soon as the workman dampens the leather.
Warble or grub holes along the back are not likely to be found in hides taken from cattle killed in the summer or fall.
A hide that has been cut by the butcher should never be used for harness leather.
When a butcher cuts the animal's throat from ear to ear, the hide is shortened because the cheeks are severed from the body, which damages the hide in length.
There are two general methods of tanning: the sole leather method, which makes leather firm and hard, and the upper leather method, which makes leather pliable and tough.
The sole leather method of tanning secures greater weight, but its quality is unsuited to the harness maker.

Leather tanned partly by the sole leather method can be detected while working it by its hard character; it does not work well in rounds or when being raised, and is more likely to break under a sudden strain.
Short-tanned leather is leather that coils like a piece of tin and shows a pale streak through the center when cut.
Limy leather is leather with a loose, wrinkled grain, or puffed up beyond its proper thickness, which stretches and falls away to its natural substance when worked.
Black-oak tanned leather shows a greenish-yellow appearance in spots on the flesh side; it is soft and has less strength than white-oak leather.
"Gum", "spew" and "fry" are different local names for the same fault in leather, caused by the use of poor oils and grease in currying.
Leather that has been well curried has a surface free from roughness or wrinkles and feels smooth and silky to the touch.

Hard leather is sometimes moistened by the currier to make it feel mellow and appear tough. The dampness can be detected by placing the palm of the hand on the thickest part of the side. Such leather shrinks in weight and is a poor purchase.
Leading harness manufacturers who make full lines never cut a harness from a single side; they use a specific grade or weight of leather for each particular strap.
Leading custom harness manufacturers purchase or cut only backs of the best quality.

Using the splitting machine to get lighter stock costs extra labor, wastes leather, and materially weakens the strap, because the part of the flesh side that is removed is the strongest part of the stock.
A harness maker who keeps a full line of weights from six to twenty pounds a side has leather for every requirement except the heaviest truck harness.
Light weights are needed for bridles whatever kind of harness is made; as a rule, sides weighing fourteen pounds and under can be cut to good advantage for bridles.
Traces, back-bands and breeching-straps require heavier leather than other parts, and hides suitable for these straps should always be kept on hand.
Light road harness of the best quality, single or double, is made up of two thicknesses and stitched throughout.
For light road harness the leather should weigh fourteen to sixteen pounds to the side for the harness proper and eight to twelve pounds to the side for the bridles.
Track harness, a popular style for trotting horses, is made up of single straps throughout, except the back-bands.
For track harness the leather should come from fine-grained young hides weighing about sixteen pounds to the side for all parts but the bodies.
The bodies of a track harness should be of lighter weight leather, or they must be skived off on the under side to prevent the edges curling up.
Bridles for track harness should use the same weight of leather as bridles for light road harness, that is eight to twelve pounds to the side.
The medium grade of light single harness is generally made up with single straps and lined points, and its best leather weight is sixteen to eighteen pounds to the side, except for the bridle.
Leather of sixteen to eighteen pounds to the side answers for all grades of single or double harness up to those requiring one and one quarter inch traces.
For light coach harness the best leather weight is about eighteen pounds to a side.

If extra heavy traces are used on light coach harness, it is better to choose leather heavy enough that only two thicknesses are needed, which avoids a filling-in piece. If a filling-in piece is used, it should be of quite light leather.

For coach and coupe harness, straps other than traces, hold-backs, back-bands, breeching-straps and bridles should be cut from sides of eighteen to twenty pounds, and the bridles from sides of about fourteen pounds.
Light express harness is made up of single straps and requires sides weighing eighteen to twenty pounds each.
Sides of eighteen to twenty pounds also answer well for farm harness and the lighter grades of team harness.
Heavy truck and cart harness requires the heaviest grades of leather in the market.
The recommended leather weights for each kind of harness refer to the average spread of oak-tanned sides; extra large or small hides, or hemlock-tanned hides, must be gauged from them.
Grain leather is much used for folds; the bellies, or the lower portions of trimmed hides, usually answer well for this purpose.
The finest grain leather for the folds of coach and light harness is made from sides weighing sixteen pounds or under, while team and truck harness need a heavier grade.
